articles.title: New units
articles.content: FOLLOWING the interior minister’s recent remarks on new administrative units, there has been much discussion in political and intellectual circles on the topic. It seems that the powers that be are pressing for administrative devolution. Earlier, they had favoured local governments and often attempted to transfer decision-making powers and resources to the lower tiers. Is the current push the same approach in different packaging? While we frequently hear about smaller provinces and administrative units , cities, towns and rural locations are not mentioned. The fact is that cities, especially large urban regions, need a special arrangement for governance, resource allocation and service delivery. If the current rulers sincerely want a workable reset, then this aspect must be factored in. Future devolution plans must begin with a gradual reduction in the number of cantonment administrations. Ap­­proximately  four dozen cantonments exist across the country, especially in the larger cities. Many view them as administrative and developmental anomalies. Residents and civil administrations complain that these areas are not aligned with urban development initiatives. Their planning and zonal control must, therefore, be given to local regulatory authorities to facilitate uniform policymaking and planning. All neighbourhoods under federal land management agencies must also fall under local land management bodies. Moreover, the definition of urban and rural structures cannot be left to provincial governments. We have seen that, over the years, no effective and innovative effort has been made to bring about institutional reforms. Our urban development authorities are merely poor upgrades of colonial improvement trusts. A visit to any municipal office takes one back to the 19th century. Modern, efficient and accountable institutions are long overdue. Similarly, capable tehsil and taluka administrations must focus on the betterment of small farmers, entrepreneurs, industries and digital businesses. One would hate to see our peasants bowing before corrupt and cruel feudals. Cities must be allowed to look after their own governance issues. The sway that provincial governments have over city administrations must also be phased out. Large and medium cities must be empowered to tackle their own administrative, economic and governance challenges. In addition, a desperately needed overhaul of the police department can neither be overlooked nor postponed. The growing law-and-order challenges in many parts of the country, particularly Karachi, cannot be addressed without a competent and locally accountable police force. If law enforcers continue to serve the influential, then reform will remain a pipe dream. Cities and local units should be effectively empowered when it comes to taxation. The transfer of resources through national and provincial financial commissions should be carried out through a just and transparent mechanism. It is ironic that while hundreds of new projects are announced and their foundation stones are laid with tremendous fanfare, a sound method for the maintenance of existing infrastructure is nowhere in sight. An oft-discussed aspect of the new design is that the restructuring will be an irreversible process. Therefore, a pragmatic, large-scale approach for the benefit of urban and rural populations is crucial, particularly for poor communities in underdeveloped areas. It is hoped that the anticipated administrative makeover will be initiated through planned procedures around a comm­o­nly shared vision for durable impro-vement and prog­ress. There should also be new platforms for experts’ participation in the development of our urban and rural regions. Cities are the seats of our civilisation and engines of progress. If we fail to give direction to their growth and sustenance, we will not have a future. Besides, cities are our common habitat. Therefore, the opinions of experts from a variety of disciplines and the aspirations of every cross-section of society need to be accommodated to shape consensus on what Pakistan’s cities and adjoining regions should look like. Certain elements see the rise of cities, urban culture and the attainment of an urban identity as politically undesirable. It must be remembered that the recognition of all cities as units of effective administration is the first step towards acknowledging the dreams of youth and especially women. Millions of young people in this country can live a decent life with a sense of purpose if Pakistan has a collection of large, medium and small cities and rural areas that are capable of providing good opportunities, safety, education and essential facilities. This is not unattainable. The writer is an academic and researcher.
articles.author: Dr Noman Ahmed

articles.title: Protecting privacy
articles.content: IT has been two decades since British mathematician Clive Humby coined the phrase ‘data is the new oil’. The world’s largest companies — from Google to Facebook and Apple — were amassing large amounts of data on user desires and behaviour. This meant that these companies increasingly had more and more power to predict how people would behave. Think of it like a massive intelligence network to which users were willingly giving information about themselves all day. In Pakistan, people do not always take these risks seriously. The assumption is that because Pakistan is not as heavily digitised as the West, there is less reason to worry about who has your data and what they do with it. The idea that one’s identity and the data attached to it is accessible to someone else is not something that has worried a lot of Pakistanis. Companies like Apple and Amazon that together have so much data on so many consumers in the West do not yet have that kind of penetration in Pakistan. As a result, these two behemoths, who have information on everything from a consumer’s heartbeat and activity and sleeping habits to the food present in his refrigerator, do not dominate the Pakistani consumer’s life. However, Pakistan is fast moving towards digitisation and connecting identity to behaviour. One of the earlier examples of this is the Computerised National Identity Card (CNIC), which, today, is necessary for everything — from owning a cellular phone to opening a bank account. A couple of decades ago, the shanakhti card was rarely used unless one had to get a driving licence or register a marriage, or do something similar. Now a CNIC number is required across the board for banking, travel, buying property, university admissions, etc. Pakistanis are increasingly turning to electronic banking and entrusting their data to networks and servers to access their money. However, according to at least one cybersecurity analyst the systems used by even some top financial institutions can be hacked. A password system was tested to reveal how reliance on old-style passwords, instead of passphrases, could constitute a vulnerability in the system. This is because AI-fuelled and OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) credential guessing make it easy to crack passwords. Pakistan hasn’t kept pace with the demands of data protection. Furthermore, the absence of two-factor authentication — which “verifies a user’s identity by asking for two pieces of proof, such as an online account password and a one-time passcode” —  is not routinely enforced across many digital platforms, including apps and websites, in the country. This means that it is easy for someone else to log into your account and potentially steal your money. It is especially easy for criminal elements who use unsecured Wi-Fi networks to harvest data which is being transmitted. The point is that data is increasingly important and Pakistan is behind the times when it comes to its protection. CNIC numbers can be fraudulently utilised by criminals — who are guilty of stealing one’s legal identity — for all kinds of unlawful activities. At the moment, Pakistan has not legislated on data protection. As lawyer Salma Khan noted in her article earlier this month, the Personal Data Protection Bill has been languishing in parliament since 2018. Consequently, there are no minimum standards with which financial institutions and utility companies that have your data must comply in order to protect your information. This means that, in the absence of a set policy of complia­nce, companies have no incentive to in­­vest in foolproof cybersecurity for their customers. Fortunately, the courts have given us some hope. In a recent landmark decision pertaining to bank fraud, the Lahore High Court ruled, according to a report, that “customer data entrusted to a bank constitutes ‘property’ under the law and its dishonest misuse may amount to criminal breach of trust”. According to the court, bank employees who had access to sensitive financial information could be held liable for its misuse. While this is helpful, it still leaves consumers very vulnerable to someone other than bank employees misusing that data. As Pakistan digitises and data becomes a powerful resource (like oil) it is imperative that people understand the consequences of the information they transmit, enter and freely provide to companies via the internet. Knowing who you are, what you do, where your money is and what you desire is all possible just by looking at your phone. And those who know everything about you can, in the end, control what you do. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.rafia.zakaria@gmail.com
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: The beneficiaries of war
articles.content: WARS are generally assessed through a binary lens. Strategic analysts, policymakers and the media tend to focus on a simple question — who won and who lost? The recent US-Iran war has generated a similar debate. Has Washington been able to achieve its objectives? Has Iran successfully withstood American military pressure and preserved its capacity to resist? But this binary framework overlooks another, often more consequential, dimension of modern warfare. Wars do not merely produce military winners and losers. They also redistribute wealth, accelerate technological change and create commercial opportunities for industries positioned to profit from insecurity. In the case of the US-Iran conflict, the most obvious beneficiaries may ultimately be neither Washington nor Tehran. The two capitals have both paid a substantial price. They have expended military resources, suffered economic disruption and experienced varying degrees of tactical and strategic pain. The conflict may therefore produce no clear geopolitical victor. Yet several sectors have emerged as unmistakable commercial winners. The foremost beneficiary of the US-Iran conflict has been the defence industry. Modern wars consume extraordinary quantities of missiles, interceptors, drones, precision-guided munitions and other military equipment. Every missile fired has to be replaced. Every depleted stockpile creates new procurement requirements. Every perceived vulnerability generates pressure for additional defence spending. The financial results of major US defence companies illustrate this dynamic. Several sectors have emerged as unmistakable commercial winners in the US-Iran conflict. Lockheed Martin reported earnings of $1.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, compared with $342 million during the same period in 2025. Its sales increased by 11 per cent to $20.1bn, while its backlog reached a record $230bn. Sales in its missiles and fire control segment increased by 19pc to $4.1bn. Similarly, RTX, the parent company of Raytheon, reported Q2 2026 net income of $2.139bn, up from $1.657bn in the corresponding quarter of 2025. Raytheon sales increased by 18pc to $8.269bn, supported by demand for systems such as Patriot, Standard Missile and AMRAAM. A prolonged conflict not only increases the immediate consumption of weapons but also generates a second wave of demand, ie, replenishment of stockpiles. The conflict between the US and Iran has resultantly become a multi-year procurement cycle for these firms. The longer the insecurity persists, the more governments feel compelled to order additional weapons, ammunition and defensive systems. For the military-industrial complex, geopolitical instability can translate into expanding order books. Select firms in the energy sector have been another major beneficiary. The US-Iran war, combined with uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and disruptions to regional energy flows, created precisely the conditions in which large oil companies, refiners and commodity traders tend to thrive on higher prices, supply uncertainty and extreme market volatility. The figures are striking. ExxonMobil’s Q2 2026 net income reached $14.5bn, compared with $7.08bn in the corresponding period of 2025, which is an increase of almost 105 pc. Similarly, Chevron’s earnings increased dramatically, while Marathon Petroleum, Phillips 66 and Valero Energy also recorded major gains as higher energy prices and refining margins transformed geopolitical disruption into exceptional financial returns. The trend was not confined to the US. Shell reported Q2 2026 profits of $9.84bn, compared with $4.26bn in Q2 2025, while British Petroleum reported $5.7bn, compared with $2.34bn during the corresponding period. TotalEnergies, Saudi Aramco, Glencore and Trafigura also benefited from the extraordinary volatility created by the conflict and the resulting disruption in energy markets. The point is not that every energy company automatically benefits from every war. Conflict can also destroy infrastructure, disrupt production and create substantial risks. But the US-Iran war demonstrates how supply disruptions and uncertainty can produce extraordinary gains for companies capable of trading volatility, refining crude and exploiting higher prices. For many firms, instability itself can become profitable. The beneficiaries of modern conflict are no longer limited to companies manufacturing tanks and missiles. Warfare is increasingly dependent on artificial intelligence, cloud computing, satellite data, cybersecurity and real-time battlefield analysis. Palantir Technologies has emerged as one of the glaring examples of this transformation. In Q2 2026, the company generated revenue of $1.94bn, representing 93pc year-on-year growth. Revenue from the US government reached $809m, an increase of 90pc. Microsoft also secured a five-year Pentagon contract worth $9.69bn for Microsoft 365, cloud subscriptions and other services for the US military and intelligence community. At the same time, the Pentagon has been pushing AI companies to expand their capabilities into classified networks, creating new opportunities for firms capable of developing secure AI systems for military and intelligence purposes. The US-Iran war may therefore accelerate a structural transformation in the military marketplace. Global shipping industry is another example of war-generated profits. Disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz forced vessels to alter routes and created enormous uncertainty in global shipping markets. The resulting increase in freight rates transformed tanker operations into a highly profitable business. Frontline and Scorpio Tankers are some prominent examples with record Q1 and Q2 earnings of 2026. There are also less visible beneficiaries. Defence consultants, geopolitical risk firms, intelligence service providers, private security contractors and an expanding ecosystem of digital media personalities have all found that geopolitical crises generate unprecedented demand for their products, services and content. Although, decisions on war and peace are determined by governments, it is equally difficult to ignore the political economy associated with prolonged warfare. This raises an uncomfortable question: if war creates exponential profits for some industries, would they prefer the settlement of conflicts or their prolonged continuation? The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.X:@itskhurramabbas
articles.author: Khurram Abbas

articles.title: Dynamics of reorganisation
articles.content: WHILE debating the question ofcarving out more ‘administrative units’from Pakistan’s existing four provinces, we may find it relevant to study how India has reorganised its states (equivalent to our provinces) since independence. The example is pertinent because of the shared circumstances of the two countries created out of undivided India. They inherited the same interim constitution — the Government of India Act, 1935 — which each adapted to fit its own context. Both countries chose a parliamentary form of government. Pakistan adopted a more explicit federal character, while India shied away from calling itself a federation. Instead, it opted to describe itself as a ‘union with some federal characteristics’. Probably, India’s more diluted form of federalism helped it carve an uncomplicated path for creating new provinces: a simple majority in parliament and a non-binding consultation with the concerned states. On the other hand, Pakistan’s 1973 Constitution made the creation of new provinces contingent upon the passage of a resolution in the concerned provincial assembly or assemblies by a two-thirds majority before the bill for new provinces could be tabled in parliament and passed in the two Houses by a two-thirds majority. This set the bar very high for altering the boundaries of the provinces as compared to India. Around the time of Partition, undivided India consisted of 14 provinces and 587 princely states, of which two provinces (Bengal and Punjab) were partitioned. Both India and Pakistan received a part of each province. Three provinces — Sindh, the North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) and British Balochistan — joined Pakistan, taking the tally of provinces in India and Pakistan to 11 and five respectively. Thirteen princely states acceded to Pakistan. The rest either voluntarily acceded to India or were coerced into doing so through brute military force. Kashmir has remained a disputed territory ever since. The reorganisation of Indian states was triggered by language riots after a political activist, who had been demanding a separate state from Madras for Telugu-speaking people, died in 1952 following a fast unto death. When the riots spread, the Government of India fast-tracked the creation of the Telugu-speaking Andhra state (later called Andhra Pradesh) out of Madras state. The demands for more states based on language spread. The Indian government constituted a three-member States Reorganisation Commission in December 1953, headed by a former judge of the supreme court. As Pakistan debates new provinces, India’s experience offers relevant insights. The commission, constituted to propose the redrawing of state boundaries, also came to be known as the Justice Fazal Ali Commission after the chairman. Its proceedings continued for about 21 months and it submitted its report in September 1955. Parliament finally passed the States Reorganisation Act in 1956, leading to the redrawing of boundaries and the creation of 14 states and six union territories. Language was a major consideration but not the only one in the creation of the states. The creation of the new states continued even after the enactment of the States Reorganisation Act. Four years later, Bombay state was split into the Gujarati-speaking Gujarat state and the Marathi-speaking Maharashtra. After persistent demands by the tribes, Nagaland was carved out of Assam state in 1963 because of its distinct language and culture. Indian Punjab was split into three parts, with Punjabi-speaking Punjab, Hindi-speaking Haryana and the hilly northern tracts merged into Himachal. In all, 15 new states were created or upgraded from union territories after the enactment of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. In the meantime, some areas were downgraded to union territories; the latest such move saw the illegal splitting of Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir into the two ‘union territories’ of Ladakh and Jammu & Kashmir in 2019. The latest tally is 28 states and eight union territories. As stated earlier, most of the new states and union territories were created on the basis of identity such as language, ethnicity, culture and geography, or the difference in the level of development in two parts of a state. There is hardly a case where a state was created just because of its large population. Uttar Pradesh, with an estimated population of over 243 million, is a case in point. The state’s population almost matches the population of Pakistan. The population of the US has increased 10 times since 1863, but not a single state has been carved out of the existing ones since then. The last state created this way was West Virginia, which had seceded from Virginia in 1863 during the Civil War. What are the lessons from the two-country case studies above? The first is that population on its own is not enough of a reason to split a province into two or more units. Pakistan’s population has increased four times since 1973, but this alone may not justify the creation of more provinces. There may be merit in the proposal to create more provinces, but such reorganisation should be studied in depth, preferably by a commission or even a parliamentary committee as was done when the 18th Constitutional Amendment was being drafted. The concentration of too many powers in the provinces is a key issue that needs to be addressed. Creating more provinces may not be the best solution for this problem as it will not only be an expensive exercise but may also create political instability in one or more provinces. The problem, in my opinion, may be solved by creating a balance of powers among the three tiers of the state — federal, provincial and local. This balance can be effectively achieved by empowering local government through a comprehensive constitutional amendment, as India did in 1993. The LGs already have elaborate infrastructure and staff, unlike the proposed new provinces. The proposed amendment should not only guarantee adequate powers for various tiers of local government but should also ensure the direct transfer of funds to LGs from the National Finance Commission. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.president@pildat.orgX:@ABMPildat
articles.author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob

articles.title: History revisited
articles.content: THE government’s decision to expand its Unesco World Heritage list from 25 to 37 sites is a welcome move that promises to boost our global heritage profile and generate tourism opportunities. The latest additions — Bazira-Barikot, the Bhamala Buddhist Complex, Sethi House, the Mai Qamro Mosque, Pharwala Fort, the Kalasha Valley Cultural Landscape and the Gor Khatri Archaeological Complex among them — symbolise this region’s multiple rebirths. Pakistan’s historical wealth — from fortified edifices to living traditions — is a part of its civilisational legacy. Sadly, criminal cartels have long exploited poor law enforcement and economic frailty to plunder treasures, especially in Punjab and KP. More inscriptions will go a long way towards stemming the erosion of ancient marvels. Antiquity is a celebration of diversity. It also maps our identity. In Pakistan, regrettably, even restoration work triggers concern as it is merely cosmetic and hardly an exercise in transparency, accountability, cooperation and respect for academic opinion. Science, and engagement with historians and international preservation experts, must guide our efforts to save historical bequests. Additionally, specialised training, modern methods, tightened borders and site security are vital to prevent damage and theft. Climate-related destruction has exposed already vulnerable sites, while poverty forces the underprivileged to resort to illegal excavations. Meanwhile, rules are meaningless unless they are faithfully implemented. Persistent danger to the most precious parts of this land imperil Pakistan’s position as it pursues wider respect on the world heritage stage. Archaeologists have for decades unearthed the layers of time hidden in Kushan, Buddhist, Roman, Ghaznavid, Scythian, and Mughal remains. The fact that just one site — Peshawar’s Gor Khatri — bears the imprints of 13 civilisations shows how essential it is for Pakistan to demonstrate sustained political commitment towards preserving the past for future generations.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Passing on relief
articles.content: ON Wednesday, Ogra announced a Rs32.63 reduction in high-speed diesel prices — from Rs395.69 to Rs363.06 per litre — alongside a Rs2.97 increase in petrol prices. It presented the move as major relief for the public. It is, in a sense. Diesel prices have a broad impact because the fuel is widely used by heavy transport, power plants and large generators. Yet, real relief will materialise only if the reduction in diesel prices translates into corresponding lower transport and freight fares and, in turn, cheaper everyday goods, particularly food. Pakistan’s fuel pricing follows a familiar pattern. When diesel prices go up, transporters, wholesalers and retailers quickly raise fares and prices, blaming higher diesel costs even before the increase has taken full effect. But when fuel prices come down, the savings are rarely passed on to consumers as quickly. Before reducing their own prices, businesses across economies similar to ours often wait to see whether a cut in fuel prices will last. The problem is more pronounced in Pakistan where government institutions have limited capacity to ensure that lower fuel costs are passed on to consumers. Freight charges, intercity bus and city fares, the prices of food and other essential commodities such as vegetables, cement and steel were all increased when fuel prices rose earlier this year as hostilities broke out between the US and Iran. But these higher charges have not come down even though diesel rates have declined by almost a third of their peak of Rs520.35 per litre in April. Provincial governments play a crucial role here: they approve fares, while district price-control authorities are responsible for monitoring prices in the markets and shops. In practice, however, both systems have largely been reactive, responding to public complaints rather than proactively checking whether transport fares and retail prices have fallen in line with lower fuel costs. In fact, the track record of the provinces in enforcing downward revisions after fuel cuts is weak. Consumer prices and transport fares have rarely moved down, and even if they have it has been hardly more than a symbolic move, despite a significant decline in fuel rates. For consumers to benefit, the provinces must ensure that transport, freight and food prices fall within days, and not weeks. They have the legal authority to act but do not seem to possess the will to do so.
articles.author: Editorial
